value.overview: The Keel-billed Toucan (Ramphastos sulfuratus), also called the Rainbow-billed Toucan, is a large, colorful forest bird recognized by its enormous multicolored bill, black body, yellow throat, and red undertail. It lives from southern Mexico through Central America to northern Colombia and northwestern Venezuela. In Costa Rica it is a familiar resident of lowland and foothill forests, especially on the Caribbean slope. Its fruit-eating habits make it an important disperser of seeds in tropical forests.
value.classification: The Keel-billed Toucan belongs to the toucan family Ramphastidae and the order Piciformes. It is one of the larger toucans and is closely related to other Ramphastos species, including the Chestnut-mandibled Toucan.
value.identification: Adults are about 46 cm long and have a black body, bright yellow throat and breast, red undertail coverts, blue skin around the eye, and a very large bill marked with green, blue, orange, red, and black. The bill is light and partly hollow despite its size. In Costa Rica, it can be distinguished from the larger Chestnut-mandibled Toucan by its vividly rainbow-colored bill rather than a mainly yellow bill with a chestnut lower mandible. Sexes look alike.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama to northern Colombia and northwestern Venezuela. In Costa Rica it is a resident, occurring mainly in humid lowland forests and foothills, particularly on the Caribbean slope, and locally reaching about 1,200 to 1,400 m. It also uses forest edges, secondary growth, partially open woodland, clearings with scattered trees, plantations, and gardens when fruiting trees and suitable nesting or roosting cavities remain available.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally non-migratory across its range. It may make local movements between forest patches or follow seasonal fruit supplies, but it does not undertake a regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding is reported mainly from January through May. Pairs nest in natural cavities or old woodpecker holes in trees and may reuse suitable cavities. A clutch usually contains two to four white eggs. Both adults share incubation and care of the chicks. The young hatch after roughly 16 to 20 days and remain dependent in the nest for several weeks while their bills and flight abilities develop.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit forms most of the diet, including fruits from many tropical trees and shrubs. The toucan usually feeds in the canopy, plucking fruit with the tip of its bill and tossing it backward before swallowing. It also takes insects, small lizards, tree frogs, bird eggs, and nestlings, especially when additional protein is needed. Undigested seeds may be regurgitated or passed intact, helping disperse plants through the forest.
value.behavior: Keel-billed Toucans are active during the day and often travel or feed in small groups, commonly moving from tree to tree through the canopy. Their flight consists of rapid wingbeats followed by gliding, while movement among branches is usually by hopping. They are vocal and social but may defend fruiting trees from other toucans. At night, several birds may roost together in tree cavities, folding their tails over their backs to fit inside.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining globally, with habitat loss and degradation contributing to reduced populations in parts of its range.
conservation.threats: The main concerns are continuing loss and fragmentation of tropical forest, removal of large trees that provide food and nesting cavities, and local capture or hunting. Habitat conversion for agriculture, pasture, roads, and development can reduce the connected forest areas the species needs. In Costa Rica, protecting mature trees and maintaining links between forest remnants are important for resident populations.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native forest, especially lowland and foothill habitat, while retaining large fruiting trees and cavity-bearing trees. Support protected areas and habitat corridors in Costa Rica, avoid purchasing wild-caught toucans, and report illegal wildlife capture or trade to the appropriate authorities. Responsible birdwatching and planting native fruiting species can provide additional habitat and encourage conservation of local forest ecosystems.
